scheme: five-point biased-upwind advection on a uniform axial grid; Dirichlet inlet c_l(z=0)=0; stiff BDF integration with an analytic Jacobian sparsity pattern
note: This is convergence of the PDE DISCRETISATION, which is a different quantity from the rate-parameter-grid convergence already reported. The late fraction is reported alongside the whole cup because it is the most discretisation-sensitive of the three sub-intervals and the temporal argument depends on fraction shape.
solver_warnings: scipy emitted 6 RuntimeWarnings during the sweep (4 'overflow encountered in multiply', 2 'invalid value encountered in multiply'), all from `scipy.integrate._ivp.common.num_jac` -- the NUMERICAL Jacobian estimator. The solver supplies a Jacobian SPARSITY pattern but not an analytic Jacobian, so scipy estimates entries by finite differences and its step-size heuristic can overflow on the stiffest cells. They are recorded rather than suppressed. They do not affect the reported values: every cell agrees with the reference to <= 0.021 %, and the profile minimum is identical in all nine, which would not hold if a failed Jacobian estimate had corrupted an integration.
reading: The PDE discretisation is CONVERGED at the production configuration, by a wide margin. Across 3 axial resolutions (100/200/400 nodes) x 3 solver tolerances (1e-5/1e-6/1e-7), the whole-cup concentration varies by at most 0.0004 %, the late fraction -- the most discretisation-sensitive of the three sub-intervals -- by at most 0.0013 %, and the profile range ratio by at most 0.0204 %. The location of the profiled-objective minimum is IDENTICAL (0.884) in all nine cells. The identifiability conclusion is therefore not an artefact of the numerics: the broad, boundary-reaching near-optimal set is a property of the design and the data, not of the mesh or the integration tolerance. Notably even 100 axial nodes reproduces the 400-node answer, so the production grid of 200 is already well beyond what these outputs require.
scheme_attribution_note: The implementation's docstring attributes the five-point biased-upwind stencil to Carver & Hinds (1978). That attribution is NOT carried into the manuscript or the reference list, because it is not recorded on the pannusch2024 source card and its bibliographic metadata has not been verified here. Citing it requires an author to check the reference; the scheme is described by name meanwhile, which is what the review asked for.
